questions.why: The verb קָם is pa'al, and the feminine present adds ־ָה: קָמָה. An hour takes בְּ and needs no word for o'clock: בְּשֶׁבַע.
No word for 'is' in the present: הֶחָתוּל רָעֵב is already a sentence. תָּמִיד can stand before or after the adjective.
Both are hitpa'el: the מִתְ in front, and an action you do to yourself. The feminine present ends in ־ֶת.

questions.q: I don't like to be late.
questions.why: The negative לֹא goes before the verb, and 'to be late' is one word, the infinitive לְאַחֵר. A woman says אוֹהֶבֶת.
The verb רָץ is the masculine present of לָרוּץ; she would be רָצָה. לְ and הַתַּחֲנָה merge into לַתַּחֲנָה.

questions.q: The street is empty and there are no cars.
questions.why: 'There are no' is אֵין, with no verb after it and no article on what is missing.

questions.q: Today is Saturday, and there is no bus.
questions.why: Hebrew says הַיּוֹם שַׁבָּת, today Saturday, with nothing for 'is'. אֵין covers 'there is no'.

questions.q: She is looking for the keys in the bag.
a: היא מחפשת [את המפתחות בתיק|בתיק את המפתחות]
questions.why: The keys are definite, so they take אֶת. בַּתִּיק is בְּ and הַתִּיק, the ה swallowed into the vowel.
Hebrew is happy with 'the coat' where English says 'her coat', and הַמְּעִיל שֶׁלָּהּ is right too. Definite, so אֶת.

questions.q: The cat is already asleep on the bed.
questions.why: The one word יָשֵׁן is 'sleeps', 'is sleeping' and 'is asleep': Hebrew has one present. כְּבָר usually comes before the verb.

questions.q: The cat is waiting for its breakfast.
a: החתול מחכה [לארוחת הבוקר|לארוחת בוקר|לארוחת הבוקר שלו]
questions.why: The verb לְחַכּוֹת takes לְ for what you wait for. In smichut the article goes on the second noun: אֲרוּחַת הַבּוֹקֶר.

questions.q: The keys are under the newspaper, next to the phone.
questions.why: The word מִתַּחַת takes לְ, and לְ with הָעִיתּוֹן becomes לָעִיתּוֹן. לְיַד takes its noun straight after it.

questions.q: In the kitchen she makes coffee and two slices of bread.
a: בַּמִּטְבָּח הִיא עוֹשָׂה קָפֶה וּשְׁתֵּי פְּרוּסוֹת לֶחֶם.
[במטבח היא|היא במטבח] [עושה|מכינה] קפה ו[שתי|2] פרוסות לחם
היא [עושה|מכינה] קפה ו[שתי|2] פרוסות לחם במטבח
questions.why: The noun פְּרוּסָה is feminine, so two is שְׁתֵּי, the form that sits in front of a noun. וְ before a sheva becomes וּ.

questions.q: Where are my keys? I can't find them.
a: אֵיפֹה הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת שֶׁלִּי? אֲנִי לֹא מוֹצֵא אוֹתָם.
איפה המפתחות שלי אני לא [מוצא|מוצאת|מצליח למצוא|מצליחה למצוא|יכול למצוא|יכולה למצוא] אותם
questions.why: 'Them' after a verb is אוֹתָם, the object marker with an ending. Where English says 'can't find', Hebrew is happy with plain לֹא מוֹצֵא.

questions.q: Finally she understands: today is Saturday.
questions.why: The verb מְבִינָה is the feminine present of לְהָבִין, a hif'il: the מְ in front is the sign. After 'understands' Hebrew may add שֶׁ, 'that'.
